html:
The oracle of Apollo at Delphi, on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, where a priestess called the Pythia spoke the god's answers to questions. It was the most respected oracle in the Greek world from about the 8th century BCE.

Cities asked it before founding colonies, during the age of Greek colonisation, before going to war and before changing their laws. Kings sent gifts; Croesus of Lydia was told that if he attacked Persia a great empire would fall, and it was his own. Sayings such as "Know yourself" were carved at the temple.

Control of the sanctuary mattered. The First Sacred War put it under a league of states, and the Pythian Games were held there. Treasuries and statues, like the Charioteer of Delphi, filled the site. Delphi survived the Gallic attack of 279 BCE, but declined under Rome and was closed under Theodosius I in the late 4th century CE.
